1	# Svalboard — Hands Down Neu + Arensito symbols
2	
3	Vial keymap for the Svalboard Lightly, ported from my Glove80.
4	
5	## Load it
6	
7	1. Open [KeyBard](https://captdeaf.github.io/keybard/) with the Svalboard plugged in.
8	2. **Load** → `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil`.
9	
10	No reflash — Vial writes the keymap live.
11	
12	Needs `/dev/hidraw*` to be readable, which it isn't by default. The udev rule is
13	in `system/etc/udev/rules.d/92-vial.rules`. Without it, KeyBard and Vial both see
14	the keyboard and then silently fail to open it.
15	
16	## Layers
17	
18	Each finger sits in a cup with five switches: **N**orth, **S**outh, **E**ast,
19	**W**est and **C**enter (the plain down-press). East is screen-right on both
20	hands, so West is inward on the right hand and outward on the left.
21	
22	### Layer 0 — Hands Down Neu
23	
24	```
25	             W    N     C     S     E
26	  L pinky    tab  w     r     x     -
27	  L ring     ~    f     s     c     @
28	  L middle   (    m     n     l     v
29	  L index    g    p     t     d     b
30	  R index    ,    .     a     u     :
31	  R middle   /    q     e     o     )
32	  R ring     ;    "     i     y     &
33	  R pinky    z    '     h     k     j
34	```
35	
36	The alphas are Hands Down Neu as it sits on the Glove80 — note `;` on the right
37	inner column where upstream publishes `-`.
38	
39	Two places this departs from a literal port, both because the Svalboard has four
40	fingers per hand and the layout assumes five columns:
41	
42	- **`g` is on the index's West.** Hands Down gives the left index the whole
43	  inner column (`v`/`b`/`g`). Only two fit on an index cup, so it keeps `b` and
44	  `g` and exiles `v` — the rarest — to the middle finger.
45	- **`z`, `j` and `tab` are on laterals.** They live in outer columns the
46	  Svalboard doesn't have. `tab` gets the left pinky's West, x=0.0, the outermost
47	  point of the hand.
48	
49	Brackets are deliberately *not* on this layer; Arensito has them. Seven symbols
50	*are*, placed by measured frequency rather than by feel — counted over hand-typed
51	prompts and shell history (agent-driven sessions excluded) and over code authored
52	here, per 1000 characters:
53	
54	| | `-` | `:` | `(` `)` | `&` | `@` | `~` |
55	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
56	| code | 11.6 | 9.3 | 4.9 | 0.68 | 0.17 | 0.22 |
57	| hand-typed | 33.5 | 5.1 | 0.30 | 0.17 | 0.01 | 0.12 |
58	
59	- `-` → **left pinky East.** The clear winner on both counts.
60	- `:` → **right index East**, the strongest free lateral. Was shift+`;`.
61	- `(` `)` → **left middle West / right middle East**, an outward-facing mirror
62	  pair, so `()` alternates hands. They earn a base key from code only.
63	- `&` → **right ring East.** The rarest thing on this layer bar `@`, on one of
64	  the worst keys here, which is the point. Ring laterals are the hardest cups to
65	  reach.
66	- `@` → **left ring East**, the other ring lateral, and the slot `g` vacated. It
67	  is rarer than `&` by 6× in code and 19× typed, so frequency alone would leave
68	  it on `MO(1)`. It gets promoted because the promotion is free: both ring
69	  laterals were empty, so one bad key displaces nothing and still beats two good
70	  ones. East is the inward of the two; West stays free.
71	- `~` → **left ring West**, the lateral `@` left open, on the same argument. By
72	  `freq.py` it is 0.12/1k hand-typed against `@`'s 0.06 and 0.22 in code against
73	  `@`'s 0.33 — the same order of magnitude, ahead on the typed side. It suits a
74	  bad key for a reason a rate does not show: 338 occurrences hand-typed, **zero**
75	  of them consecutive repeats, longest run 1. You hit `~` once at the front of a
76	  path and leave, and a key you never hit twice in a row is the right thing to
77	  put somewhere awkward.
78	
79	`*` was considered and rejected: it looks like 6.7/1k in code, but 90% of that
80	is `**` in markdown prose, and it is 0.03/1k in anything hand-typed.
81	
82	`` ` `` was considered and rejected for the opposite reason — it is the
83	strongest candidate on the board and there is nowhere to put it. At 8.34/1k
84	hand-typed and 3.58 in code it outranks `:` and `(`, which both hold good keys.
85	But the only free slot was a ring lateral, and *nothing frequent goes on a ring
86	lateral*; worse, backtick comes in pairs around inline code spans, so that slot
87	would be the worst key here hit twice per span. It stays on `MO(1)` at the left
88	pinky's West, which is at least a left-right alternation against the right-thumb
89	`MO(1)`. Promoting it would mean demoting a letter — `z`, `q` and `j` are the
90	only cheaper occupants left — and a thumb hold mid-word for "jazz" or "quiz" is
91	worse than the hold it would save.
92	
93	`@`'s two numbers come from a later counting pass than the other four columns —
94	in that same pass `&` read 1.10 and 0.19, so read the gap between the two, not
95	the absolute against the older columns. Most of even that 0.17 is `@types/…`
96	imports and `git@github.com`, which are completed rather than typed.
97	
98	Each is promoted, not copied — all seven are holes on layer 1, so nothing sits on
99	two keys. Six of those holes are in Arensito's own grid; `~`'s is on a lateral,
100	which is why the lateral list below is one shorter than it was.
101	
102	### Layer 1 — Arensito symbols (hold `MO(1)`)
103	
104	```
105	  { } [ ] ·   · · < > $
106	  ; / · 0 ·   \ 1 · · =
107	  6 7 8 9 +   * 2 3 4 5
108	```
109	
110	Ported from the Glove80 `symbols` layer. `·` is a dead key — Arensito puts
111	`-`, `:`, `&`, `@`, `_`, `(` and `)` there, and all seven are one-key elsewhere
112	now (see layer 0 and the thumbs below). They're dead rather than transparent on
113	purpose: falling through would type `n`, `.`, `e`, `i`, `b`, `v` and `/` from
114	the middle of the symbol layer.
115	
116	The grid above is on N/C/S; the
117	laterals carry the six symbols Arensito leaves out, which would otherwise cost
118	`MO(1)`+shift+key:
119	
120	```
121	  ` on the left pinky        ! on the left index
122	  % on the left ring         # on the left middle
123	  | on the right index       ^ on the right middle
124	```
125	
126	`~` used to sit beside `` ` `` on the left pinky's East, paired with its
127	unshifted partner. It is on the base layer now, and its old lateral is dead
128	rather than transparent — falling through would type `-`.
129	
130	`?` isn't here on purpose — it's shift+`/`, and `/` is on the base layer.
131	
132	`_` gets a second seat on the **left thumb's space key**. Arensito's own `_` is
133	on the right index's North, the same hand as `MO(1)`; on space it's a
134	left-right roll instead. Space itself isn't typeable while `MO(1)` is held —
135	every other thumb stays transparent, so shift, ctrl, enter and backspace still
136	work on the layer.
137	
138	### Layer 2 — navigation (hold `MO(2)`)
139	
140	Arrows four-across on the right hand, innermost to outermost, matching Glove80
141	base-layer positions 75–78:
142	
143	```
144	  R index  R middle  R ring  R pinky
145	     ←        ↓        ↑        →
146	```
147	
148	F1–F12, home/end, pgup/pgdn, volume and play/pause fill the rest.
149	
150	`MO(2)` is on the right thumb's **nail** so that `alt` can be held with it — see
151	"Thumbs" below. Everything else on the layer is a right-hand finger, so shift,
152	ctrl and GUI reach it from the left thumb without contortion.
153	
154	### Layer 15 — mouse
155	
156	Svalboard's firmware switches here by itself when the pointing device moves, and
157	leaves on the first key that isn't on this layer. **Nothing reaches it by
158	keypress, by design.** Buttons 1/3/2 sit on index/middle/ring South of both
159	hands; `USER06` is `SV_RECALIBRATE_POINTER`.
160	
161	### Thumbs
162	
163	The cluster is not six keys laid out in space. It is six switches hit by
164	different **parts of the same thumb**, and the `.vil` column index — which *is*
165	mirrored between hands, unlike the x coordinate — names them:
166	
167	| col | part | left | right |
168	|---|---|---|---|
169	| 0 | knuckle | ctrl | **alt** (one-shot) |
170	| 1 | nail | gui | **`MO(2)`** |
171	| 2 | down | shift | `MO(1)` |
172	| 3 | pad | space | bspc |
173	| 4 | up | esc | enter |
174	| 5 | double-down | delete | ralt |
175	
176	`pad` is the community favourite and holds the most-pressed thumb key on each
177	hand. `down` takes the heaviest hold. `knuckle` is the worst key on the cluster
178	and is exactly where a modifier belongs. `up` strains under heavy use, so it
179	gets taps rather than holds.
180	
181	**One thumb holds one of these at a time.** The exception is a *fat-finger*
182	pair, of which knuckle+nail is the reliable one — the only way a single thumb
183	holds two thumb keys at once.
184	
185	That is the whole reason `MO(2)` sits on the nail. It used to be on `up`, and
186	that made `alt`+arrow — `alt+shift+down`, `ctrl+alt+left`, all of them — not
187	awkward but **unpressable**: alt is on the knuckle, and no thumb reaches knuckle
188	and up together. Moving `MO(2)` to the nail puts it on alt's fat-finger partner
189	and costs only `enter`, which took `up` in exchange. Enter is a tap and pays
190	`up`'s strain once; `MO(2)` is a hold and was paying it for the length of every
191	arrow key.
192	
193	**Alt is a one-shot**, `OSM(MOD_LALT)`, because one chord partner is not enough.
194	The knuckle pairs with the nail and nothing else, so alt can chord with exactly
195	one right-thumb key — and `MO(2)`, `enter` and `bspc` all want to be it. Sticky
196	alt sidesteps the whole problem: tap it and it holds for the next key, so
197	`M-RET` and `M-DEL` work without a chord at all. `M-DEL` has never been
198	available on this layout by any other route — backspace is on the pad. Holding
199	it is unchanged, so `alt+tab` still cycles.
200	
201	That is one of the three fixes the Svalboard community names for this squeeze.
202	The other two don't fit here: **one layer hold per thumb** (this layout has both
203	on the right) and **bottom-row mods**, "because south is so good on sval" —
204	South is alphas here. The underlying rule being broken is *modifiers on one
205	thumb, layer switches on the other*: `alt`, `MO(1)` and `MO(2)` are all on the
206	right. Shift, ctrl and GUI escape it by being left-thumb keys. Alt can't follow
207	them; the left thumb's six seats are full.
208	
209	Note `OSM(MOD_LALT)`, not `OSM(KC_LALT)` — Vial accepts both, but they are
210	different keycodes (`0x52A8` vs `0x52E3`) and the latter reloads as raw hex.
211	
212	`double-down` is not a sixth position. It is the `down` key pressed harder, the
213	DataHand deep press. That is why nothing you press in a hurry goes there — `gui`
214	sat on both and was unusable, `tab` was tried and was worse. They now hold
215	`delete` and `ralt`. Those two slots were found empirically, as "the only
216	positions with no free side", well before the mechanism had a name.
217	
218	`space` left and `bspc` right match Glove80 positions 69 and 74 — Svalboard's own
219	configs ship those mirrored.
220	
221	## Printable cheatsheet
222	
223	```sh
224	python3 cheatsheet.py   # writes cheatsheet.html
225	```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read the Svalboard's own vial.json out of the keyboard (Vial cmd 0xFE 0x02)."""
import fcntl, glob, lzma, os, struct, sys

HIDIOCGRAWINFO = 0x80084803
HIDIOCGRDESCSIZE = 0x80044801
HIDIOCGRDESC = 0x90044802

VID, PID = 0x303A, 0x4044
RAW_USAGE_PAGE, RAW_USAGE = 0xFF60, 0x61


def raw_info(fd):
    buf = bytearray(8)
    fcntl.ioctl(fd, HIDIOCGRAWINFO, buf, True)
    bus, vid, pid = struct.unpack("Ihh", bytes(buf))
    return bus, vid & 0xFFFF, pid & 0xFFFF


def report_descriptor(fd):
    size = bytearray(4)
    fcntl.ioctl(fd, HIDIOCGRDESCSIZE, size, True)
    n = struct.unpack("I", bytes(size))[0]
    buf = bytearray(4 + 4096)
    buf[0:4] = struct.pack("I", n)
    fcntl.ioctl(fd, HIDIOCGRDESC, buf, True)
    return bytes(buf[4:4 + n])


def is_raw_hid(desc):
    """True if the top-level collection is usage page 0xFF60, usage 0x61."""
    i, page, usage = 0, None, None
    while i < len(desc):
        b = desc[i]
        size = b & 0x03
        size = 4 if size == 3 else size
        tag, typ = b >> 4, (b >> 2) & 0x03
        data = int.from_bytes(desc[i + 1:i + 1 + size], "little") if size else 0
        if typ == 1 and tag == 0x0:      # Global: Usage Page
            page = data
        elif typ == 2 and tag == 0x0:    # Local: Usage
            usage = data
        elif typ == 1 and tag == 0xA:    # Main: Collection
            return page == RAW_USAGE_PAGE and usage == RAW_USAGE
        i += 1 + size
    return False


def find_device():
    for path in sorted(glob.glob("/dev/hidraw*")):
        try:
            fd = os.open(path, os.O_RDWR | os.O_NONBLOCK)
        except OSError:
            continue
        try:
            _, vid, pid = raw_info(fd)
            if (vid, pid) == (VID, PID) and is_raw_hid(report_descriptor(fd)):
                return path, fd
        except OSError:
            pass
        os.close(fd)
    return None, None


def xfer(fd, payload):
    import select
    os.write(fd, b"\x00" + bytes(payload).ljust(32, b"\x00"))
    r, _, _ = select.select([fd], [], [], 2.0)
    if not r:
        raise TimeoutError("no response from keyboard")
    return os.read(fd, 32)


def main():
    path, fd = find_device()
    if fd is None:
        sys.exit("no Svalboard raw-HID interface found")
    print(f"# {path}", file=sys.stderr)
    size = struct.unpack("<I", xfer(fd, [0xFE, 0x01])[:4])[0]
    print(f"# compressed vial.json: {size} bytes", file=sys.stderr)
    blob = b""
    for block in range((size + 31) // 32):
        blob += xfer(fd, [0xFE, 0x02] + list(struct.pack("<H", block)))
    sys.stdout.write(lzma.decompress(blob[:size]).decode())


main()

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions:

- **Never run a reviewer in the background.** Do not set `run_in_background`,
  do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is out. A backgrounded
  reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a finished turn, and the
  run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it blocking and read its
  verdict in the turn you dispatched it.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path. Exit codes: 0 clean, 3 findings, 2 timeout, 1 error — **only 0
   is clean**, and a reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the four.
   Re-dispatch rather than report its silence.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral.**
   Per finding: quote it, then name the edit answering it by file or write down
   why you are not making it.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

Condensed from a real decision: a 320-line spec, a client call in 19 minutes
where three people read it aloud, a $45,000 sign-off, the lead writing
*"just send it."* Reviewer output is illustrative, not a transcript.

❌ **What this looks like when it fails:**

> They are going to read it out loud section by section — that *is* the review,
> and a review pass first is a second reading of something nobody has read
> once. The lead said send it. Sending.

✅ **What it looks like when it holds:**

> Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this
> done. The "second reading" framing conflates two reads: theirs is for fit,
> the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant.
> "Just send it" is a scheduling call; the retry semantics are mine. Moving the
> call:

```
$ drovr code-review run warehouse-sync spec
reviewed 320 lines (a41c9e2..HEAD) · 4/4 angles returned
correctness    IMPORTANT §4.2 retry window (30s) < the 45s ack timeout in §3.1
error-handling IMPORTANT §6 reconciliation excludes the partial-day boundary
type-design    nit       §2 names two ids for one endpoint
exit 3
```

> Both Importants fixed in `spec/warehouse-sync.md` — retry window 30s → 60s, §6
> reconciliation now spans the boundary day — from `spec-review.json`, not the
> summary line. A spec has no suite, so step 6 here is both edited
> sections re-read against §3.1, not assumed. The nit is deferred
> and recorded here: the duplicate id is in a section the client wrote, and
> renaming it would confuse the walkthrough. Sent 22 minutes late, call moved:
> that window would have shipped a contract we could not meet.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.

content.text:
Done — `b61478c`, pushed.

**Right thumb double-down → `TO(0)` on layer 15.**

Why an exit key was needed at all: "leaves on the first key that isn't on the layer" isn't a way out, because eight cups are taken (index/middle/ring South both hands, both pinky Centers). Type `d f c r u o y h` first and it clicks or recalibrates — the layer leaves, having eaten the keystroke.

Three decisions worth knowing:

1. **No Svalboard keycode does this.** I dumped the keyboard's own `vial.json` over the Vial protocol (`0xFE 0x02`) — all twenty `USER*` codes are pointer settings, scroll modes, layer toggles. The nearest, `SV_TOGGLE_AUTOMOUSE`, kills auto-activation entirely rather than dismissing one visit.
2. **`TO(0)`, not `TO(15)`** — this one would have bitten. QMK's auto-mouse intercepts a `TO()` aimed at the mouse layer and reads it as *pin this layer on*. `TO(0)` isn't intercepted, so it's a plain `layer_move(0)`; `auto_mouse_layer_off()` reads real layer state, not a cached flag, so the next pointer move brings the layer back.
3. **Right, not left.** Right double-down is `ralt` — least missed while a hand's on the pointer. Left keeps `delete` on purpose: select with the pointer, hit delete, and the delete both lands *and* leaves. An exit key there would swallow it.

Declared by physical x through `thumb_col()` like every other thumb override, so the hardware-geometry guard covers it; `check_labels()` forced the cheatsheet glyph ("type").

Review: drovr panel, `80372e5..b61478c`, 4/4 angles clean — each names the files it read. Build reproduces byte-identical.

**Heads up:** the layout I printed last turn is stale — `475c84f` landed between turns and re-placed the symbols by search. Left middle South is `f` now, ring North `v`, right middle West `-`.

Next: reload `SvalHandsDownNeu.vil` in KeyBard, nudge the trackball, and press right double-down — it should drop straight back to typing without emitting anything.
